well-architect.ntfs-allocation-action-summary2: Please note the following important considerations:
well-architect.ntfs-allocation-downtime-warning-content: It is crucial that you schedule this task during a maintenance window to minimize disruptions to your operations. This process could involve data loss and downtime. To prepare, carefully verify that all data has been backed up, and ensure that all files and data are moved to a different drive before starting the reformatting process.

well-architect.ntfs-allocation-optimization-steps3: Format one drive at a time.
well-architect.ntfs-allocation-optimization-steps4: Select 64K in the Allocation unit size drop-down menu.
well-architect.ntfs-allocation-optimization-steps5: Repeat steps 1-4 for all SQL Server drives (Data, Log, TempDB).

well-architect.heartbeat-setting-action-summary1: Cluster heartbeat settings need adjustment to prevent unnecessary failovers.
well-architect.heartbeat-setting-action-summary2: The default heartbeat and threshold cluster settings are designed for highly tuned on-premises networks and don't consider the possibility of increased latency in a cloud environment due to network latency or failure, maintenance, or hitting resource bottlenecks. The heartbeat network is maintained with UDP 3343, which is traditionally far less reliable than TCP and more prone to incomplete conversations.
well-architect.heartbeat-setting-action-summary3: Therefore, when running cluster nodes for SQL Server on AWS EC2, change the cluster settings to a more relaxed monitoring state to avoid transient failures.
well-architect.heartbeat-setting-what-will-happen: The cluster heartbeat settings will change as following:
well-architect.heartbeat-setting-what-will-happen-conte: SameSubnetThreshold will be set to 40 heartbeats.
CrossSubnetThreshold will be set to 40 heartbeats.
CrossSiteThreshold will be set to 40 heartbeats.
SameSubnetDelay will be set to 1000 milliseconds.
CrossSubnetDelay will be set to 1000 milliseconds.
CrossSiteDelay will be set to 1000 milliseconds.

well-architect.mtu-alignment-note1: A brief disruption to active network connections is expected.All ongoing sessions (such as RDP, SSH, SMB, SQL, or file transfers) will be temporarily interrupted while the network interface is reconfigured.New connections can be established once the change is complete (usually within a few seconds).
well-architect.mtu-alignment-note2: No changes will be made to FSxN.If you require a different MTU for FSxN, you must recreate the file system in a VPC/subnet with the desired MTU setting.
well-architect.mtu-alignment-note3: It is recommended to perform this operation during a scheduled maintenance window to minimize impact on users and applications.

severity-description.0-9: Informational messages that return status information or report errors that aren't severe. The Database Engine doesn't raise system errors with severities of 0 through 9.
severity-description.10: Informational messages that return status information or report errors that aren't severe. For compatibility reasons, the Database Engine converts severity 10 to severity 0 before returning the error information to the calling application.
severity-description.11: Indicates that the given object or entity doesn't exist.
severity-description.12: A special severity for queries that don't use locking because of special query hints. In some cases, read operations performed by these statements could result in inconsistent data, since locks aren't taken to guarantee consistency.
severity-description.14: Indicates security-related errors, such as permission denied.
severity-description.15: Indicates syntax errors in the Transact-SQL command.
severity-description.16: Indicates general errors that can be corrected by the user.
severity-description.17: Indicates that the statement caused SQL Server to run out of resources (such as memory, locks, or disk space for the database) or to exceed some limit set by the system administrator.
severity-description.18: Indicates a problem in the Database Engine software, but the statement completes execution, and the connection to the instance of the Database Engine is maintained. The system administrator should be informed every time a message with a severity level of 18 occurs.
severity-description.19: Indicates that a nonconfigurable Database Engine limit has been exceeded and the current batch process has been terminated. Error messages with a severity level of 19 or higher stop the execution of the current batch. Severity level 19 errors are rare and must be corrected by the system administrator or your primary support provider. Contact your system administrator when a message with a severity level 19 is raised. Error messages with a severity level from 19 through 25 are written to the error log.
severity-description.20: Indicates that a statement has encountered a problem. Because the problem has affected only the current task, it is unlikely that the database itself has been damaged.
severity-description.21: Indicates that a problem has been encountered that affects all tasks in the current database, but it is unlikely that the database itself has been damaged.
severity-description.22: Indicates that the table or index specified in the message has been damaged by a software or hardware problem. Severity level 22 errors occur rarely. If one occurs, run DBCC CHECKDB to determine whether other objects in the database are also damaged. The problem might be in the buffer cache only and not on the disk itself. If so, restarting the instance of the Database Engine corrects the problem. To continue working, you must reconnect to the instance of the Database Engine; otherwise, use DBCC to repair the problem. In some cases, you may have to restore the database.If restarting the instance of the Database Engine doesn't correct the problem, then the problem is on the disk. Sometimes destroying the object specified in the error message can solve the problem. For example, if the message reports that the instance of the Database Engine has found a row with a length of 0 in a nonclustered index, delete the index and rebuild it.
severity-description.23: Indicates that the integrity of the entire database is in question because of a hardware or software problem.Severity level 23 errors occur rarely. If one occurs, run DBCC CHECKDB to determine the extent of the damage. The problem might be in the cache only and not on the disk itself. If so, restarting the instance of the Database Engine corrects the problem. To continue working, you must reconnect to the instance of the Database Engine; otherwise, use DBCC to repair the problem. In some cases, you may have to restore the database.
severity-description.24: Indicates a media failure. The system administrator may have to restore the database. You may also have to call your hardware vendor.
